content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem now, starting with the symptom: shop pages loading slowly for shoppers, kept short and without a figure. For the causal chain, I'm first checking which evidence to cite for the slow responses, and I'm leaning toward the AL1 alert since no other series is labeled.

I'm laying out the causal chain now: requests queued because CPU hit its limit, and the rise in traffic drove that CPU use, which points to load rather than a change. I'm ruling out recent deploys and flag changes for the window before settling on that.

I'm tying the root cause to load: the service ran at a fixed CPU limit with no added capacity as traffic rose, and adding capacity is what ended the incident, so I'll fold that into the third step of the chain.

I'm settling on the root cause now: request volume to io-shop rose to several times its usual level, and the service's CPU limit could not keep up with it, so requests queued and slowed.

I'm weighing whether to note the likely per-request cost in the plain-words version, since it could explain why the load hit the CPU so hard.

I'm checking that the root cause stays within what the record shows, and I'm keeping the plain-words version to requests arriving far above their usual level with too little CPU to serve them. Next I'm noting that the scaling-out is still in place, so a similar rise in load could again use up the CPU and slow responses.

I'm checking whether the scale-out gap belongs in the record: no automatic scale-out appears as CPU use hit the limit, and the replicas stayed at their count until Argus added capacity by hand. Had capacity grown with the load, the queuing would likely have been shorter or avoided.

I'm adding the contributing factors now: the service's capacity didn't grow with the load, since no automatic scale-out showed up as CPU hit its limit, so I'll propose reviewing the autoscaling settings for io-shop. I'm also noting a possible per-request CPU cost from the account page's figure path, which could be a contributing factor and is already covered by the fix.

I'm weighing whether the missing page belongs among the contributing factors, but it doesn't change how the incident played out, so I'll record it under what went wrong and add a detection action item with no factor attached.

I'm weighing whether a slower alert delay might be a contributing factor, since the scale-out landed at the same moment the incident ended, but the five-minute wait is by design, so I'll leave it out. I'm also noticing there's no alert on CPU saturation, so the CPU hitting its limit was only caught through the latency alert.

I'm proposing three action items: automatic scale-out on io-shop tied to CPU nearing its limit, an alert on CPU use as a share of that limit so saturation gets flagged before the latency alert, and routing the latency alert to on-call paging. I also want to find out why the request volume rose in the first place.

I'm considering whether to include a closing item on where the rise in requests came from, since the record stops short of explaining it, and I'm noting that no action item covers it yet. Then I'm sorting the went-well items: the investigator's placing of onset and finding no production or flag changes, the scale-out that ended the slowdown, Argus's confirmation, and Code-Fix's draft PR. On the went-wrong side, nobody was paged, and I'm wondering whether the investigator skipped the logs.

I'm noting that the ruled-out check in step 3 cites a deploy and flag review, and I'm treating the list of assumptions as the part still to settle: that the rise in requests is real demand whose source the record doesn't show, and that the CPU limit size and autoscaling settings haven't been confirmed by any run.

I'm checking the remaining rule-outs and the step-1 wording now, keeping the figures out of the symptom description and leaving the mention of the draft pull request as just its label.

I'm checking the step on request volume: it rose to several times its earlier level, CPU use climbed with it until the load outgrew what the replicas could handle, and I'm citing only the rows that show that rise and the CPU limit, leaving out the scale-out and the verdicts that came later.

I'm settling on the symptom as shop pages slowing sharply for shoppers, and I'm placing the trigger in the third step: request volume rose far above its earlier level, and CPU use climbed with it until the replicas couldn't keep up.

action_items.item: Configure io-shop to add replicas automatically as CPU use nears its limit, with enough room for at least the peak request rate seen in this incident ({R1.3}).
Add an alert on io-shop's CPU use as a share of its CPU limit, so the service is flagged when it nears saturation and before latency climbs.
Make the HighLatency alert on io-shop page the on-call engineer.
Find where the rise in requests to io-shop came from, and whether it can happen again at this size or larger.

causal_chain.step: Responses from io-shop slowed sharply. The time within which nearly all requests are answered rose far above its usual level, so shoppers waited much longer for pages.
Requests were waiting for CPU: the service was using all of the CPU its limit allowed.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on io-shop in the day before the onset: none came back.
A flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before the investigation read the provider: none came back.
A rollout still in progress: when the deployment was read, all replicas ran one revision.

causal_chain.step: CPU use reached that limit because requests rose to several times their level before the onset and CPU use rose in step with them. That was more load than the replicas' CPU could handle.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop got far more requests than usual, more than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn.

contributing_factors.factor: No replicas were seen being added automatically as CPU use reached its limit. The service stayed at {T20.2} replicas until Argus scaled it out.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Capacity would have grown as the load did. That would have kept requests from queuing for CPU, or cut the queuing short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Each request likely cost more CPU than it needed to. Code-Fix read the files behind the account page's spending figures: the default figure, and the one behind typical-purchase-feature, both do work that grows with the square of a shopper's purchase history. Nothing has run this reading.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Cheaper requests would have let the same CPU handle more of them before they queued, so the slowdown would have been later and milder, or would not have happened.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No alert was seen when CPU use neared its limit. The slowdown was found only by the latency alert, which waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on CPU nearing its limit could have fired before latency rose this far, so capacity could have been added sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent checked for production changes and found no deploys, releases or flag changes in the window, which pointed the investigation at the load rather than at a change.
The Mitigation Agent scaled out the deployment of io-shop, and the service came back to normal.
The Mitigation Agent checked that the service was no longer at the incident's level before it judged the action confirmed.
The Code-Fix Agent opened draft pull request #529 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert did not open an on-call incident, so no person was engaged.

input.root_cause: Requests to io-shop climbed from {R1.1} to as high as {R1.3}, and CPU use climbed with them until it reached the service's CPU limit ({R2.3} at its highest). From then on the replicas had more work than CPU to do it, so requests waited for CPU and responses slowed.
input.still_at_risk: If requests rise beyond what the scaled-out replicas' CPU can handle, io-shop could run out of CPU again and slow down the same way.
input.symptom: Shop pages slowed sharply for shoppers
